title: The mind is not self-luminous (4.18–4.21)
hook: a phone screen seems to glow by itself; Patanjali says the mind only seems to

segments.voice: Yesterday, sutras 4.14 to 4.17: vastu. Your line was realism. One thing, two minds, two paths. Did you notice the color you brought to something? Day four hundred eighty-five.
screen: `REALISM. THE COLORING IS IN THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Look at the moon on a clear night and it seems to shine on its own. It doesn't. Every bit of that silver is borrowed sunlight. Without the sun, the moon is a dark rock. Now try something stranger. Notice that you know what you're thinking right now. A thought appears, and it's known. A worry shows up, and it's known. It feels as if the mind is lit from inside, glowing by itself. Patanjali says that glow is borrowed too. And he names where it comes from.
screen: `THE MOON'S LIGHT IS BORROWED.` → `A THOUGHT APPEARS, AND IT'S KNOWN.` → `BY WHAT?`

segments.voice: Sutra 4.18: the turnings of the mind are always known to their master, the purusha, because the purusha does not change. Purusha is the seer, pure consciousness, the one Patanjali has been pointing to since book one. Notice the word always. Every thought, every mood, every distraction is known, even the ones you'd rather nobody saw. And the reason given is that the knower doesn't move. A changing thing can't witness all the changes. Something has to stay still. Then 4.19, short and sharp: na tat svabhasam drishyatvat. It is not self-luminous, because it is seen. The mind is something seen, an object, like a cup or a cloud, only subtler. Things that are seen don't light themselves. They're lit. Sutra 4.20 adds that the mind can't know itself and its object in one single act. And 4.21 closes a door. If one mind were known by another mind, you'd need a third to know that one, and a fourth, forever, and memory would be a tangle. So the line has to stop somewhere, at a seer who isn't a mind at all. Why should that matter on a hard afternoon? Because if you can see the anxiety, you are not only the anxiety. The weather is real. It's being watched by something that isn't weather.
screen: `THE TURNINGS ARE ALWAYS KNOWN.` · `THE MIND IS SEEN, SO IT ISN'T THE LIGHT.` · `A MIND KNOWN BY A MIND: NO END.` · `YOU CAN SEE THE WEATHER.` · then, large: `NA TAT SVĀBHĀSAṂ DṚŚYATVĀT.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath find its own pace. Wait for a thought to come. It will. When it does, don't follow it. Just notice: this is known. Another thought: this is known too. A sound, a feeling in the chest, a plan for later: known, known, known. You don't have to find the knower. Just rest in the plain fact that each thing is seen, and let the things come and go. The bell holds the time.
Svabhasa, self-luminous — what the mind is not. It is seen, so its light is borrowed, from the purusha, the seer that does not change.
Your line: the seer knows the mind. Today, when a strong mood arrives, say to yourself, this is known, and notice there's a little room around it. Day four hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: In Yoga and Samkhya teaching, the purusha is the unchanging witness and the mind belongs to nature; teachers often use the moon's borrowed light to explain why the mind only seems to shine by itself.

fork.setup: a thought appears and it's known. what knows it, according to 4.18?
fork.reveal: the turnings are always known to their master, the purusha. a mind knowing a mind would need another, without end.

original.note: Sanskrit svābhāsa: self-shining. sva (self) + ābhāsa (light, appearance). the mind, says 4.19, is not this.

trapdoor: what you thought: I know my thoughts because my mind knows itself.
what it means: the mind is something seen; its knowing comes from the seer, who doesn't change.
what a scholar hears: 4.19 turns on drishyatva, being an object of sight; 4.21 rules out a mind known by another mind as an infinite regress with a confusion of memories.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras 4.18, 4.20–4.21 (always known to the purusha; not both at once; no mind known by another mind)

notes: The moon's borrowed light is a common teaching image, used here as the script's own illustration rather than attributed to a commentator.
Commentators read 4.18–4.21 partly as a reply to views that the mind is self-aware; the script leaves that debate out. Confirm that's acceptable.
Prabhu in 4.18 rendered 'master'; translators also use 'lord'.
